section.title: The Way of Love
section.sectionRationale: This is the most excellent way Paul promised at the end of chapter 12, set between the teaching on gifts and its application to worship. It is not a detour into poetry but the beating heart of the argument: gifts without love are worthless, love is the character that must govern their use, and love alone endures when every gift has passed away. The chapter exposes the emptiness of Corinthian pride and holds up the very character of Christ.
section.thesis: Without love the most impressive gifts are nothing, for love is patient and kind and self-giving and never fails, while prophecy, tongues, and knowledge are partial and will pass away; so faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest of these is love.
section.frameNote: Three movements: without love the greatest gifts are nothing; the portrait of what love is and is not; and love that never fails, outlasting the partial gifts, so that of faith, hope, and love the greatest is love.

verses.text: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not {{agape|love}}, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing.
Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud.
It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.
Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth.
It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

units.label: Love never fails
units.note: the greatest of these is love

verses.text: Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part,
but when the {{teleios|perfect}} comes, the partial passes away.
When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways.
Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known.
And now these three remain: {{pistis|faith}}, {{elpis|hope}}, and love; but the greatest of these is love.

agape.gloss: Self-giving, sacrificial love that seeks the good of another regardless of merit. It is not mere feeling or affection but a settled, active commitment, the love God has shown in Christ. This is the love that must govern every gift; without it the most spectacular endowment is nothing, and this love alone never fails.

teleios.gloss: Complete, mature, perfect, that which has reached its goal. When the perfect comes, the partial passes away. Read together with seeing face to face in verse 12, it points most naturally to the completeness we will know at Christ's return, when partial knowledge gives way to full sight, though its exact reference is debated.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, and reliance upon God and His promises. One of the three that remain, faith lays hold of what God has done and said. Yet even faith will one day give way to sight, whereas love endures forever, which is why Paul names love the greatest of the three.

elpis.gloss: Hope, the confident expectation of the good God has promised. Hope reaches toward what is not yet seen and sustains the believer through the present age. Like faith it belongs to this life of waiting, but love outlasts even hope's fulfillment, remaining forever the greatest.

basic.context: Between his teaching on spiritual gifts in chapter 12 and its application to worship in chapter 14, Paul unveils the most excellent way. The Corinthians prized gifts as marks of status; Paul insists that any gift, however dazzling, is worthless without love. He then paints love's character in a series of plain descriptions, and shows that while the gifts they treasured are partial and passing, love never fails. Of the three great abiding realities, faith, hope, and love, the greatest is love.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is not a stand-alone poem but part of a sustained argument; love is the answer to the pride and division that spoiled their use of gifts. The portrait in verses 4 to 7 is deliberately convicting, describing the very virtues Corinth lacked. Verses 8 to 13 set the temporary against the permanent to reorder their priorities around what will last.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is agape, self-giving love that seeks another's good, the love of God in Christ, not mere feeling. Paul says the gifts are partial until the teleios, the perfect or complete, comes, when we will see face to face. And of the three that remain, pistis, faith, and elpis, hope, belong to this life of waiting, but love outlasts them both, and so is the greatest.
basic.typology: The love described here is the character of God Himself, supremely displayed at the cross. Every line of verses 4 to 7 is fulfilled in Jesus: patient and kind, not self-seeking, bearing and enduring all things for us. The chapter is a portrait of Christ, and the pattern of the love His people are called and empowered to show.
basic.christ: Read the description of love and you are reading a description of Jesus. He is patient and kind, keeps no record of wrongs, bears all things and endures all things, and gives Himself entirely for those who did not deserve it. The love that never fails is the love that took Him to the cross. He is both the perfect embodiment of this love and the source from which His people learn to love.
basic.god: God is love, and this chapter shows what that love is like: not sentiment but sacrificial, patient, truthful, enduring commitment. The love commanded here is first the love God has for us and pours into us by His Spirit. Because love is what God is, love is what will remain when this age and its partial gifts have passed away.
basic.crossReferences: 1 John 4 says God is love and that we love because He first loved us. Romans 5 tells how God's love is poured into our hearts by the Spirit. John 13 records Jesus' command to love as He has loved. Galatians 5 lists love as the first fruit of the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: From beginning to end the Bible's story is the story of God's love pursuing a wayward people, reaching its climax at the cross and its consummation when we see Him face to face. Gifts belong to this age of partial knowing; love belongs to God's eternal nature and so endures forever. To walk in love is to live now by the reality that will fill the age to come.

context.literary:
The chapter is a carefully shaped piece of prose, often read as a poem, though its force is that of an argument. It has three movements with a different grammar in each. In verses 1 to 3 Paul speaks in the first person and uses a series of conditions: if I speak, if I have, if I give. Each condition piles up a more extreme gift, from speech to knowledge and faith to sacrifice, and each ends with a verdict of nothing: a ringing gong, I am nothing, I gain nothing. The unit climbs and the verdict does not change. In verses 4 to 7 the grammar changes completely. The speaker disappears and love becomes the subject of fifteen verbs and phrases in a row, eight of them negative and the rest positive, so that love is described by what it does and does not do. It is a portrait, built from verbs. In verses 8 to 13 the grammar changes again to time. There is a repeated now and then, in part and fully, child and man, mirror and face, and the final line brings the three things that remain.

The chapter is a hinge. It begins after 12:31, where Paul promises the most excellent way, and it ends before 14:1, where he says to pursue love and eagerly desire the gifts. Without it, the long discussion of gifts would be a list of tools, and with it they are shaped by a purpose. The gifts Paul names in verses 1 and 2, tongues, prophecy, knowledge and faith, are those of the chapters on either side, so the hymn is not a detour but the center of the argument. The repeated word never in verse 8 contrasts love with the things that pass.
context.historical:
The Corinthians esteemed eloquence and wisdom, 1:17 to 2:5, and they esteemed spiritual display. The church had factions that gathered around favorite teachers, 1:12, a believer who boasted of his freedom, 8:1 to 3, rich members who shamed poor ones at the common meal, 11:21 and 22, and a rank-ordering of gifts, chapter 12. Paul's portrait of love is, line by line, a list of what was missing. Where love is not envious and does not boast, they envied and boasted; where it is not rude or self-seeking, they went ahead at the table and each insisted on his own rights, 10:24. The chapter is therefore far less a wedding reading than a pastoral indictment.

The setting also explains the details of verses 1 to 3. The gong and cymbal were noisy instruments, and a pagan city knew them from religious processions and temples. Paul says that a person who has tongues without love has become only noise, and he does so in a city that knew exactly what religious noise sounded like. Corinth was known for its bronze work and for its mirrors, which were polished metal and gave a poor reflection, so the picture of verse 12 would have been vivid. The idea of giving all one owns to the poor and giving one's body, verse 3, would have fitted a culture of public benefaction, in which gifts to the city won honor. Paul says that even the grandest generosity done for the sake of recognition is worth nothing. The letter was written around AD 55 to a congregation that thought it already possessed the full riches of the Spirit, 4:8, and chapter 13 shows them what they still lacked.
context.canonical:
The chapter gathers up what the Bible says about love and shows it in one place. The Law summed up in loving God with everything, Deuteronomy 6:5, and loving the neighbor as oneself, Leviticus 19:18. Jesus called these the two greatest commandments, Mark 12:28 to 31, and Paul says that love is the fulfillment of the law, Romans 13:8 to 10, and Galatians 5:14. In Galatians 5:22 love heads the fruit of the Spirit, and in Colossians 3:12 to 14 it is the garment that binds the other virtues in perfect unity. Jesus gave the new commandment to love one another as He loved them, John 13:34 and 35, and 15:12 and 13 says that there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends. The picture in verses 4 to 7 can be read in that light.

The most important background to the portrait is the character of the LORD. In Exodus 34:6 He declares Himself slow to anger and abounding in lovingkindness and truth, and the first of Paul's descriptions, love is patient, is the language used of God's patience in Romans 2:4. The line about love enduring all things echoes the refrain of Psalm 136, that His loving devotion endures forever. Song of Songs 8:6 and 7 says that love is as strong as death and many waters cannot quench it. First John 4:7 to 21 states what is only implied here, that God is love and that those who love are born of God. The triad of faith, hope and love appears in 1 Thessalonians 1:3 and Colossians 1:4 and 5, a sign that Paul had a habit of summing up the Christian life in this way. In Romans 8:35 to 39 nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God, which is another way of saying that love never fails.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to see that their favorite things are not the measure of a Christian. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice are real and good, and he names them in their strongest form so that no one can say he belittles them. Yet each, without love, comes to nothing, and the nothing is stated with a plainness that does not allow an exception. He takes away their grounds for boasting without taking away the gifts.

He also means to give the word love a content that the Corinthians could not mistake. It is not a warm feeling that comes and goes, and it is not a general goodwill. He writes about it by naming what it does and does not do, and nearly every item corresponds to a fault of Corinth that he has named in the letter. They are told what to be, and at the same time what they are not.

In the third part he shifts their sense of time. Their enthusiasm assumed that they already had everything. Paul says that what they have is partial, that they see in a mirror, and that the full day is still to come. This humility is the root of love, because someone who knows he knows only in part is less likely to boast and more ready to listen. The first hearers were meant to leave with a re-ordering of priorities: seek the gifts, but pursue love first, since the gifts will end and love will not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The portrait of love in verses 4 to 7 is written in the indicative, love is patient, love is kind, and it is meant as a command, as the first words of chapter 14 show: pursue love. It tells us what love is and so what we are to be. It is not an accurate description of anyone's actual conduct, and it should not be read as a thing the church already does. We are to read it as a mirror and be honest about what we find.

It would be easy to sentimentalize the chapter. Because it is so often read at weddings, many think it describes romantic affection. In context it describes the habits of a church. Love rejoices with the truth, verse 6, and takes no pleasure in evil, so it is not the same as tolerance of everything. It bears all things, but bearing does not mean allowing abuse; the same letter tells the church to remove a man living in flagrant sin, 5:1 to 5. Believes all things and hopes all things do not mean gullible but rather a steady refusal to give up on people.

The same caution applies to verses 8 to 13. The chapter does not set love against gifts. In 14:1 Paul tells them to eagerly desire the gifts. What it does is subordinate them: use them in love, and do not seek them for status. Verse 13 does not say that faith and hope will cease, only that love is the greatest, and Scripture elsewhere shows faith and hope continuing in the age to come in the sense that we shall enjoy what we hoped for.

debates.question: What is the perfect that comes in verse 10?

views.label: The return of Christ and the age to come
views.case: Verse 12 gives the answer: then we shall see face to face and know fully, even as we are fully known. That is the language of final fellowship with God, 1 John 3:2 and Revelation 22:4. The gifts of this age pass away when that day arrives. This is the most common reading in the church and is held by both continuationists and cessationists.

views.label: The completed New Testament
views.case: Some cessationists take the perfect, a neuter word, to mean the completed body of revelation, so that the gifts of prophecy and tongues ceased when the canon closed. They argue that the word is neuter and so refers to a thing and not to a person.

views.label: The maturity of the church
views.case: A third reading takes the perfect as mature in the sense of the church's growth to completeness, as in Ephesians 4:13, and holds that the child and man of verse 11 support the idea of the church growing up.

debates.bearing: The language of seeing face to face and being fully known is hard to match to anything short of the final day, which is why most readers lean toward the first view. The wider point does not change: whichever age is meant, love outlasts the gifts.

debates.question: Is verse 3 about boasting or burning?

views.label: Boasting
views.case: Many early manuscripts have a verb that means to boast, which gives the sense that I give my body in order to have something to boast about. The BSB follows this and says that I exult in the surrender of my body. It fits the Corinthian concern with status.

views.label: Burning
views.case: A good many manuscripts read a verb that differs by one letter and means to be burned, as the BSB footnote shows: surrender my body to be burned. Some take it to refer to martyrdom.

debates.bearing: Both readings say that the most costly self-sacrifice is worthless if love is absent. The difference is whether the worry is vanity or the cost of death. The point of the verse stands in either case.

debates.question: Are the tongues of angels literal?

views.label: A hyperbole
views.case: Paul is piling up extremes: even if I speak in the tongues of men and of angels. The language is a rhetorical exaggeration, like moving mountains and knowing all mysteries in verse 2, and it does not imply that tongues are a heavenly language.

views.label: A reference to heavenly speech
views.case: Others note that in 14:2 Paul speaks of one speaking in a tongue as not speaking to men but to God, and they take the tongues of angels as a description of the gift that the Corinthians prized.

debates.bearing: The verse makes the central point under either view: even the highest speech is a noise without love.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 4 to 7 are a string of verbs, and several of them are chosen with the whole letter in mind. Makrothymei, is patient, is a compound of long and anger or passion, and it is the word of the LORD's own character in Exodus 34:6 as the Greek Old Testament has it, slow to anger, and Paul uses its noun in Romans 2:4 for God's forbearance. Chresteuetai, is kind, is a verb related to the adjective that describes the Lord in 1 Peter 2:3, good. The first two items give one passive and one active side of love: it endures what is done to it, and it does good in return.

Zeloi, envies, is from zeloo, the same root as the verb in 12:31, eagerly desire. The choice is pointed: the same verb that is used of a proper eagerness for gifts becomes envy if it is not governed by love. Physioutai, is proud, literally is puffed up, a word Paul used earlier of the Corinthians in 4:6 and 5:2, and in 8:1 he says that knowledge puffs up but love builds up. Aschemonei, is rude, is from the same root as the aschemona of 12:23, the unpresentable parts. So the body that treats its unpresentable parts with modesty is the body that does not behave without regard for others.

Logizetai, keeps no account, is the language of bookkeeping. It is the verb used for crediting or reckoning in Romans 4:8, where blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him, and in 2 Corinthians 5:19 God was not counting their trespasses. Love does not keep a ledger of wrongs, which is how God has dealt with us.

In verse 6 the verb is sunchairei, rejoices with, which is also in 12:26: if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it. Love rejoices with the truth and not with injustice. Verse 7 begins with stegei, bears, which means to cover or to put up with, and the same verb is used in 9:12 where Paul says that they bear all things so as not to hinder the gospel. The four all things form a series of bearing, believing, hoping and enduring, and the last verb, hypomenei, is the word for steadfastness under pressure.

In verse 8 love never fails, from the verb piptei, literally falls, so that love never falls to the ground, in the sense of a thing that falls out of use. The gifts, by contrast, will be set aside, from katargeo, the verb used in verses 10 and 11 for the partial passing away and for putting away childish ways. In verse 12 the dim reflection is a combination of esoptron, a mirror, and ainigma, from which we get the English enigma, a riddle or indirect image. In Numbers 12:8 the LORD speaks to Moses face to face and not in riddles, and Paul says that this is the privilege to which all believers will come. The last word of the verse is that I shall know fully, even as I am fully known, a pair built on epiginosko, a compound of the verb to know. God's knowledge of us comes first.

typology.type: The covenant love of the LORD, as in Exodus 34:6
typology.fulfillment: When the LORD passed before Moses, He proclaimed His name as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. Paul's first words, love is patient, love is kind, are an echo of that proclamation. In Christ the correspondence is complete, for in Him the patience and kindness of God are seen in a human life and in a death, Romans 5:8. The type is incomplete in that the revelation to Moses was in a name and a voice, while the fulfillment is in a person who bore all things for us, Hebrews 12:2.

typology.type: The greatest commandment and the law fulfilled by love
typology.fulfillment: Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 set love for God and neighbor at the center of the law. Paul says that love is the fulfillment of the law, Romans 13:10. The picture of 1 Corinthians 13:4 to 7 supplies the content of what that fulfillment looks like. Jesus is the one who kept the law in this way, loving God with all He was and giving Himself for others, Matthew 5:17. The type falls short in that the law commanded love and could not produce it, whereas the Spirit pours it into hearts, Romans 5:5.

typology.type: Moses speaking face to face, and the greater sight
typology.fulfillment: Numbers 12:8 says that the LORD spoke with Moses face to face, not in riddles, and Exodus 33:11 says as a man speaks with his friend. Paul says that all who are in Christ will see face to face, verse 12. The correspondence is that what was a privilege of one prophet becomes the destination of the whole church, 1 John 3:2. Moses still asked to see more and was told that no one can see God and live, Exodus 33:20, and the fulfillment is in Christ, who has made God known, John 1:18.

typology.type: The love that does not fail, as in Song of Songs 8:6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The Song says that love is as strong as death and many waters cannot quench it. The strength of love that survives death is realized in Christ, who died and rose, and in whose love nothing in all creation can separate us from God, Romans 8:38 and 39. The correspondence is real, though the Song speaks of human love and should not be forced to carry the whole meaning of the chapter. Its image is only a pointer to a love that has gone through death and out the other side.

study.christ:
It has been said that you can put the name of Jesus in place of the word love in verses 4 to 7 and lose nothing. We should say this carefully, since Paul does not write the chapter as a description of Christ but of love. Still, the church has always read it as a portrait of Him, and the reading is sound, because love, in the New Testament, is not an idea but a Person's character and a Person's act. God showed His love for us in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us, Romans 5:8. The patience of verse 4 is His patience with Peter and with the disciples who kept missing the point. The kindness is His welcome of sinners. His refusal to boast or insist on His rights is the pattern of Philippians 2:6 to 8, where He did not grasp at equality with God but emptied Himself. The words it is not self-seeking recall Romans 15:3, which says that even Christ did not please Himself.

The keeping of no account of wrongs is realized in the cross, where God in Christ was not counting our trespasses against us, 2 Corinthians 5:19. Bearing all things is the way of the Man who carried our sins in His body on the tree, 1 Peter 2:24, and who endured the cross, scorning its shame, Hebrews 12:2. And love never fails is true of the One who, having loved His own who were in the world, loved them to the end, John 13:1.

Verse 12 says that we now see dimly and then face to face. The face we hope to see is that of Christ. Paul says elsewhere that we see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6, and John says we will be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is, 1 John 3:2. Whatever the perfect is, the hope that it describes is a person.

We should guard against two errors. One is to make the chapter into a ladder of moral effort, as though by trying to be patient and kind we could earn our way to Christ. The other is to forget that the chapter is commanded of us. Because He loves, we are made able to love, and the love He gives is the very love He is, shed abroad by the Spirit, Romans 5:5.
study.god:
The chapter says nothing directly about God in verses 4 to 7, and yet it says nearly everything, because Scripture elsewhere says that God is love, 1 John 4:8 and 16. That statement is not a slogan but a doctrine about who God is. It means that love is not one attribute among others that God has, but that all that He is shows His love: His holiness, His justice, His power and His patience are the holiness and justice and power and patience of love. The portrait of love in this chapter is therefore a portrait of the character of God. The patience of verse 4 is that of the God who is slow to anger, Exodus 34:6 and 2 Peter 3:9. The kindness is that of the God whose kindness is meant to lead us to repentance, Romans 2:4. The refusal to keep a record of wrongs belongs to the God who, in Christ, does not count our trespasses against us.

The chapter also shows that God's love is truthful. Love does not delight in evil and rejoices with the truth. A God who loved without regard for truth would be indulgent; a God who was truthful without love would be a judge only. In God they are one, and in the cross they meet, Romans 3:26. This guards against two mistakes in how we think about Him: that His love means that He does not care about sin, and that His holiness means that He does not love sinners.

God's love endures. Love never fails is a statement about a God whose character does not change and whose faithfulness lasts, Lamentations 3:22 and 23. This is the ground of the believer's security. The gifts, the knowledge and even faith and hope are bound to this age, but the love of God goes on beyond it, and the believer who is held in that love is held forever, Romans 8:38 and 39.

For worship this means that the first act of the church is to receive love and not to produce it. We love because He first loved us, 1 John 4:19. A congregation that sings of the love of God and then treats its members as rivals has not understood what it sings. The right response is thanks, and then a life that begins to look like the portrait in verses 4 to 7, not by effort alone but by the Spirit's pouring of love into hearts, Romans 5:5.

crossReferences.note: Paul promises to show a most excellent way, and chapter 13 is the showing. The verb eagerly desire in this verse is related to the word for envy in 13:4, which tells us that the same eagerness can turn to rivalry unless it is ruled by love.

Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. It is the same contrast Paul draws in 13:2 and 13:4, where knowledge without love is nothing and love is not proud. It shows that the theme of the chapter is the one he has been pressing from the start of the letter.

Pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts. This is where chapter 13 ends up, and it prevents any reading that sets love against the gifts. They are to be sought, but only in the way of love, and with prophecy preferred because it builds up.

Love is the fulfillment of the law, because it does no harm to a neighbor. This puts verses 4 to 7 in the setting of the whole law, and shows that the chapter's portrait is the content of obedience to God's commands.
Love is the fruit of the Spirit and the way the whole law is kept. Here also the opposite works are named, envy, rivalry and conceit, which are the ones 1 Corinthians 13:4 and 5 rule out.

Over all these virtues put on love, which binds them together in perfect unity. Compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience are listed just before, a close companion to the list of verses 4 to 7.

Jesus gives a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you, and by this all will know that you are My disciples. The standard is His own love, and the mark of the church is its love, which is what Paul teaches Corinth to value above gifts.

God's love has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, and God shows His love by Christ dying for us while we were sinners. It says where the love of chapter 13 comes from, and shows that it is not our achievement but His gift.

God is love, and since He loved us, we ought to love one another. The invisible God is seen when His people love, and His love is made complete in us. It states in plain terms the foundation of Paul's portrait.

The LORD proclaims His own name: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and truth. The first words of the portrait, patient and kind, are an echo of this self-revelation, and the portrait is a description of God before it is a command to us.

The LORD speaks to a prophet in dreams and visions, but to Moses face to face and not in riddles. Paul uses the same contrast in verse 12, looking in a mirror now and then face to face, and says that what Moses had is the future of every believer.

Paul remembers their work of faith, labor of love and endurance of hope. The same triad of faith, hope and love is in 1 Corinthians 13:13, so Paul speaks of them here as a summary of Christian life, with love as the one that outlasts the others.

study.oneStory:
Love is the thread that holds the whole Bible together, and this chapter pulls the thread out for the reader to see. In creation God makes a world and people to share in His goodness, Genesis 1 and 2, and what moves Him is love before any need. In the fall humanity turns from love to grasping, and the first signs are envy, blame and murder, Genesis 3 and 4. The portrait of 1 Corinthians 13 reads like a deliberate reversal of Cain: love is not envious, not easily angered, takes no pleasure in evil, and does not harm a brother.

Through the story of Israel, God keeps loving a people who do not return it. The refrain of His loving devotion that endures, Psalm 136, runs through the law, the prophets and the exile, and Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife is the picture of it, Hosea 3:1. The law tells Israel to love, Deuteronomy 6:5, and the prophets say that the law written on the heart will be a work of God, Jeremiah 31:33. The Old Testament therefore leaves a question: where will love come from?

The answer is the cross. God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us, Romans 5:8, and love of the kind in verses 4 to 7 has finally been lived in a human life. At Pentecost that love is poured into hearts by the Spirit, Romans 5:5, and the church is called to be the community in which it is visible, John 13:35. Corinth was meant to be that, and the letter's long correction is a picture of how far a church can be from it and still be the church.

And the story ends in love. The partial passes away, the dim mirror is set aside, and we see face to face, verse 12. In the new creation God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3 and 4, and they see His face, Revelation 22:4. Faith will become sight and hope will become possession, so that of the three that remain, only love is left in its fullness. That is why Paul can say that it is the greatest. What we learn now in imperfect ways, in the noisy and divided churches of this age, is the language of the age to come.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the greatest gifts exercised without love?

options.text: They are nothing, and the person gains nothing.
options.note: Verses 2 and 3: without love, I am nothing and gain nothing.

options.text: They are still useful but slightly diminished.
options.note: Paul is far stronger; without love they amount to nothing.

options.text: They are acceptable as long as they help the church.
options.note: Even prophecy and self-sacrifice count for nothing without love.

options.text: They earn a reward regardless of the heart.
options.note: Without love there is no gain, whatever the outward act.

quiz.q: Which of these best captures how Paul describes love in verses 4 to 7?

options.text: Patient, kind, not self-seeking, keeping no account of wrongs, bearing and enduring all things.
options.note: This is the portrait Paul paints of love's character.

options.text: A strong feeling of affection toward those we like.
options.note: Biblical love is active and self-giving, not mainly a feeling.

options.text: Tolerance that never speaks of right or wrong.
options.note: Love rejoices in the truth; it is not indifferent to evil.

options.text: Getting what you deserve from others.
options.note: Love is not self-seeking; it seeks the good of others.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he says love never fails?

options.text: Love endures forever, while prophecy, tongues, and knowledge are partial and will pass away.
options.note: Verse 8: the gifts cease, but love remains.

options.text: That loving people will always get the response they hope for.
options.note: The point is love's permanence, not guaranteed returns from others.

options.text: That our efforts to love are always successful.
options.note: It speaks of love's enduring nature, not our flawless performance.

options.text: That love will eventually be replaced by knowledge.
options.note: The opposite: knowledge passes away, love endures.

quiz.q: What does the contrast between now and then in verse 12 describe?

options.text: Now we see dimly and know in part; then we shall see face to face and know fully.
options.note: Verse 12 contrasts present partial knowing with future full sight.

options.text: That we already know everything there is to know of God.
options.note: Paul says we now know only in part; fullness is still future.

options.text: That knowledge of God is impossible in this life.
options.note: We do know truly, but partially; the fullness comes later.

options.text: That God will never be fully known even in glory.
options.note: Then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known.

quiz.q: Of faith, hope, and love, which is the greatest, and why?

options.text: Love, because it endures forever while faith and hope belong to this life of waiting.
options.note: Verse 13 names love the greatest of the three that remain.

options.text: Faith, because it is how we are first saved.
options.note: Faith is vital, but Paul names love as the greatest here.

options.text: Hope, because it looks to the future.
options.note: Hope endures for now, but love is called the greatest.

options.text: They are exactly equal in every respect.
options.note: Paul explicitly ranks love as the greatest of the three.

questions: Paul says even the most impressive gifts are nothing without love. Where are you tempted to measure your spiritual life by ability or achievement rather than by love?
Read verses 4 to 7 slowly, putting your own name in place of the word love. Which lines expose where you most need to grow?
Love keeps no account of wrongs. Is there a record of grievances you are holding against someone that love would call you to release?
The gifts you value most belong to this passing age, but love endures forever. How might that reorder what you give your energy to this week?
Every line describing love is true of Jesus toward you. How does receiving His patient, self-giving love free you to love others that way?

translationNotes.note: Love throughout the chapter translates agape, self-giving love that seeks another's good; it is not mere affection or feeling but active, sacrificial commitment, the love God shows in Christ.

The perfect renders teleios, the complete or mature; in light of seeing face to face in verse 12 it most naturally points to the completeness of the age to come, though some take it as the completed revelation of Scripture.
A dim reflection as in a mirror reflects the polished bronze mirrors of the ancient world, which gave a real but imperfect image; the contrast is present partial knowledge versus future full sight.
